name: Woodrow Wilson
summary: American scholar and later US President whose 1887 essay founded public administration as a separate field of study.

name: Frank J. Goodnow
summary: American scholar who gave the politics-administration dichotomy its classic form in Politics and Administration (1900).

name: Leonard D. White
summary: American scholar who wrote the first textbook of public administration (1926).

name: Frederick Winslow Taylor
summary: American engineer known as the father of scientific management.

name: Henri Fayol
summary: French mining engineer and manager who set out the elements and fourteen principles of management.

name: Luther Gulick
summary: American classical theorist who coined POSDCORB and co-edited Papers on the Science of Administration with Lyndall Urwick.

name: Max Weber
summary: German sociologist whose ideal type of bureaucracy is the starting point of organisation theory.

name: Elton Mayo
summary: Australian-born Harvard researcher whose work on the Hawthorne studies founded the human relations school.

name: Mary Parker Follett
summary: American thinker on constructive conflict, power and the law of the situation; a bridge between classical and human relations thought.

name: Chester I. Barnard
summary: American telephone executive who saw the organisation as a cooperative system and authority as resting on acceptance.

name: Herbert A. Simon
summary: American behavioural scientist who made decision-making the core of administration; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1978.

name: James G. March
summary: American organisation theorist who co-wrote Organizations (1958) with Simon and the garbage can model.

name: Fred W. Riggs
summary: American scholar of comparative and development administration, known for the prismatic-sala model.

name: Douglas McGregor
summary: American management thinker known for Theory X and Theory Y.

name: Abraham Maslow
summary: American psychologist known for the hierarchy of needs.

name: Frederick Herzberg
summary: American psychologist known for the two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory and job enrichment.

name: Chris Argyris
summary: American organisation theorist known for the immaturity-maturity theory and for work on organisational learning.

name: Rensis Likert
summary: American social psychologist known for participative management, the four systems of management and the linking pin.

name: Peter Drucker
summary: Austrian-born management thinker who introduced management by objectives.

name: Dwight Waldo
summary: American scholar who challenged value-free administration and sponsored the first Minnowbrook conference (1968).

name: Vincent Ostrom
summary: American scholar who led the public choice approach in public administration and argued for democratic administration.

name: William A. Niskanen
summary: American economist who modelled bureaucrats as budget maximisers.

name: Christopher Hood
summary: British scholar who coined the term New Public Management (1991).

name: David Osborne
summary: American writer who, with Ted Gaebler, set out entrepreneurial government in Reinventing Government (1992).

name: Robert B. Denhardt
summary: American scholar who, with Janet V. Denhardt, proposed the New Public Service as an alternative to New Public Management.

name: Charles E. Lindblom
summary: American political scientist who set out incrementalism, or 'muddling through', in policy-making.

name: Yehezkel Dror
summary: Israeli policy scientist who proposed the optimal model of policy-making.

name: Amitai Etzioni
summary: Sociologist who proposed mixed scanning in decision-making and classified organisations by the type of compliance they use.

name: Harold D. Lasswell
summary: American political scientist who founded the policy sciences and defined politics as who gets what, when, how.

name: David Easton
summary: Canadian-born American political scientist who gave the systems model of politics used in policy analysis.

name: John W. Kingdon
summary: American political scientist who gave the multiple streams model of agenda-setting.

name: Aaron Wildavsky
summary: American scholar of budgeting and policy implementation, known for the incremental view of budgeting.

name: A.V. Dicey
summary: British jurist who defined the rule of law and contrasted it with French droit administratif.

name: John M. Gaus
summary: American scholar who introduced the ecological approach to public administration.

name: Robert K. Merton
summary: American sociologist who analysed the dysfunctions of bureaucracy.

name: Gunnar Myrdal
summary: Swedish economist who called South Asian states 'soft states'; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1974.

name: David McClelland
summary: American psychologist known for the theory of needs for achievement, power and affiliation.

name: Victor Vroom
summary: Psychologist who gave the expectancy theory of motivation.

name: Fred E. Fiedler
summary: Psychologist who gave the contingency model of leadership.

name: Robert R. Blake
summary: American management theorist who developed the Managerial Grid with Jane Mouton.

name: Kautilya
summary: Ancient Indian statesman and author of the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft and administration.
note: Dates contested; usually placed in the Maurya period (c. 4th century BCE).

name: Paul H. Appleby
summary: American administrator who reported on Indian public administration in 1953 and 1956.

name: The Study of Administration
summary: Argues for a science of administration separate from politics, borrowing efficient methods from Europe while keeping democratic control.

name: Politics and Administration
aliases: Politics and Administration: A Study in Government
summary: Argues that politics expresses the will of the state and administration executes that will.

name: Introduction to the Study of Public Administration
summary: The first textbook of public administration; treats administration as management, with efficiency as its aim.

name: The Principles of Scientific Management
summary: Argues that scientific study of each task, not rule of thumb, raises output and serves both workers and management.

name: General and Industrial Management
aliases: Administration Industrielle et Générale|General and Industrial Administration
summary: Sets out the five elements of management and fourteen principles of administration.
note: French original 1916; English translations 1929 and 1949.

name: Papers on the Science of Administration
summary: Classical essays prepared for the Brownlow Committee, including Gulick's 'Notes on the Theory of Organization', which set out POSDCORB.
note: Co-edited by Gulick and Lyndall Urwick.

name: Economy and Society
summary: Weber's posthumous treatise on economy, authority and society; contains his analysis of legitimate authority and bureaucracy.
note: German original 1922 (posthumous); English editions 1947 (partial) and 1968 (full).

name: The Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization
aliases: Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization
summary: Uses the Hawthorne findings to argue that workers' social and emotional needs shape output more than pay and physical conditions.

name: Dynamic Administration
aliases: Dynamic Administration: The Collected Papers of Mary Parker Follett
summary: Posthumous collection of Follett's papers on constructive conflict, the giving of orders, power, control and coordination.
note: Edited by Metcalf and Urwick; editions are dated 1940 to 1942.

name: The Functions of the Executive
summary: Treats the organisation as a cooperative system that the executive keeps in balance through communication, incentives and accepted authority.

name: The Proverbs of Administration
summary: Article arguing that the classical principles of administration come in contradictory pairs, like proverbs, and so cannot guide action.

name: Administrative Behavior
aliases: Administrative Behavior: A Study of Decision-Making Processes in Administrative Organization
summary: Makes decision-making the heart of administration, studying it through factual and value premises and the limits of rationality.

name: The Ecology of Public Administration
summary: Lectures arguing that administration can be understood only within its social, economic, political and cultural setting.

name: Administration in Developing Countries: The Theory of Prismatic Society
summary: Sets out the prismatic society and its sala administration, marked by heterogeneity, formalism and overlapping.

name: The Human Side of Enterprise
summary: Contrasts Theory X and Theory Y assumptions about people at work and argues for management by integration and self-control.

name: Personality and Organization
summary: Argues that formal organisation keeps workers passive and dependent, in conflict with the needs of the mature adult personality.

name: New Patterns of Management
summary: Draws on Michigan research to show that supportive, group-based participative management gives better results.

name: The Administrative State
summary: Shows that American public administration theory rests on political values, challenging the claim of value-free efficiency.

name: The Intellectual Crisis in American Public Administration
aliases: Intellectual Crisis in American Public Administration
summary: Argues that the Wilson-Weber theory of bureaucracy has failed and proposes democratic administration built on public choice.

name: Bureaucracy and Representative Government
summary: Models bureaucrats as budget maximisers who push their agencies' budgets and output beyond what voters want.

name: Reinventing Government
aliases: Reinventing Government: How the Entrepreneurial Spirit Is Transforming the Public Sector|Osborne and Gaebler
summary: Sets out ten principles of entrepreneurial government, such as steering rather than rowing and meeting the needs of the customer.
note: Co-written by David Osborne and Ted Gaebler.

name: The Science of 'Muddling Through'
summary: Argues that policy makers move by successive limited comparisons from existing policy, not by comprehensive rational analysis.

name: The Policy Sciences
aliases: Policy Sciences: Recent Developments in Scope and Method
summary: Volume containing Lasswell's essay 'The Policy Orientation', which launched the policy sciences as a problem-oriented, multi-disciplinary field.
note: Edited with Daniel Lerner.

name: A Systems Analysis of Political Life
summary: Treats the political system as turning environmental inputs of demands and supports into authoritative outputs, with feedback.

name: The Politics of the Budgetary Process
summary: Shows that budgeting is incremental and political: each budget starts from last year's base and changes a little through bargaining.

name: Implementation: How Great Expectations in Washington Are Dashed in Oakland
summary: Study of a federal jobs programme in Oakland showing how many clearance points and actors defeat policy implementation.
note: Co-written by Jeffrey Pressman and Aaron Wildavsky.

name: Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution
summary: Sets out parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law, and holds that England has no separate administrative law like France's.

name: Arthashastra
summary: Treatise on statecraft covering the king, ministers, officials, revenue, espionage, law and foreign policy.
note: Date contested (often placed c. 4th century BCE); rediscovered by R. Shamasastry, who published it in 1909.

name: Public Administration in India: Report of a Survey
summary: Survey that ranked India's government among the most advanced, and led to the O&M Division and the Indian Institute of Public Administration (1954).
note: A second Appleby report on public enterprises followed in 1956.

name: Politics-administration dichotomy
summary: The view that politics decides policy and administration carries it out, so administration can be a neutral, separate field.
note: Wilson raised it in 1887; Goodnow gave it its classic form in 1900.

name: POSDCORB
summary: Gulick's acronym for the chief executive's work: planning, organising, staffing, directing, co-ordinating, reporting and budgeting.
note: Coined by Gulick (not Urwick); it builds on Fayol's elements of management.

name: Scientific management
summary: Taylor's method of finding the one best way of work through time study, standard tools and methods, scientific selection and training, and incentive pay.

name: Fourteen principles of management
summary: Fayol's principles, including division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain and esprit de corps.

name: Ideal type of bureaucracy
summary: Weber's model of rational administration: hierarchy, rules, specialised offices, written files, impersonality and full-time officials appointed on merit.

name: Types of legitimate authority
summary: Weber's three types of authority: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational; bureaucracy is the purest form of legal-rational authority.

name: Human relations school
aliases: Human relations theory|Human relations approach|Human relations movement
summary: Approach holding that informal groups, morale and workers' social needs shape output more than physical conditions and pay.

name: Constructive conflict
summary: Follett's view that conflict is best settled by integration, a solution meeting both sides' desires, rather than by domination or compromise.

name: Acceptance theory of authority
summary: Barnard's view that authority lies in the subordinate's acceptance of an order, not in the position of the person who gives it.

name: Zone of indifference
summary: The range of orders a subordinate accepts without questioning them; Simon later called it the zone of acceptance.
note: Barnard's term; Simon's 'zone of acceptance' is the same idea.

name: Bounded rationality
summary: Simon's idea that limits of information, time and mental capacity stop decision-makers from finding the best choice.

name: Satisficing
summary: Choosing the first option that is good enough rather than the best; Simon's 'administrative man' satisfices while 'economic man' maximises.

name: Fact-value dichotomy
summary: Simon's split between factual premises, which can be tested, and value premises, which cannot; he used it in place of the politics-administration dichotomy.

name: Prismatic society
summary: Riggs's model of a transitional society between fused (traditional) and diffracted (modern) types, where old and new structures coexist.

name: Sala model
summary: Riggs's name for administration in a prismatic society, where formal rules coexist with family, caste and other particular ties.

name: Theory X and Theory Y
summary: Theory X assumes people dislike work and must be controlled; Theory Y assumes they can enjoy work, seek responsibility and direct themselves.

name: Hierarchy of needs
summary: Maslow's five levels of need: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation; a need that is met stops motivating.
note: First set out in 1943; developed in Motivation and Personality (1954).

name: Two-factor theory
summary: Herzberg's theory that hygiene factors such as pay and conditions only prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as achievement and recognition motivate.

name: Immaturity-maturity theory
summary: Argyris's view that people grow from passive, dependent immaturity to active, independent maturity, but formal organisations keep them immature.

name: Four systems of management
summary: Likert's scale from exploitative-authoritative (System 1) through benevolent-authoritative and consultative to participative group (System 4), the most effective.

name: Management by objectives
summary: Managers and staff agree clear objectives together, and performance is reviewed against them.

name: New Public Administration
summary: Movement from the 1968 Minnowbrook conference stressing relevance, values, social equity, change and client focus over efficiency alone.
note: Linked with Waldo, Marini and Frederickson rather than with one founder.

name: Public choice approach
summary: Applies economics' self-interested chooser to government, favouring many overlapping agencies, competition and citizen choice over one large hierarchy.
note: Builds on Buchanan and Tullock's The Calculus of Consent (1962).

name: New Public Management
summary: Reform model bringing private-sector methods into government: performance targets, output control, markets, contracting out and separate agencies.
note: Term coined by Christopher Hood in 'A Public Management for All Seasons?' (1991).

name: Entrepreneurial government
aliases: Reinventing government model|Steering rather than rowing|Catalytic government
summary: Osborne and Gaebler's model of government that steers rather than rows and is competitive, mission-driven, results-oriented and customer-driven.

name: New Public Service
summary: The Denhardts' alternative to NPM: government should serve citizens rather than customers and help them build a shared public interest.
note: Article version 2000; book The New Public Service: Serving, Not Steering 2003.

name: Incrementalism
aliases: Incremental model|Disjointed incrementalism|Successive limited comparisons|Partisan mutual adjustment
summary: Lindblom's model in which policy changes in small steps from existing policy, agreed through partisan mutual adjustment among groups.

name: Optimal model
summary: Dror's model joining rational analysis with extra-rational elements such as judgement and intuition, plus meta-policy-making and learning from feedback.

name: Mixed scanning
summary: Etzioni's third approach to decisions: a broad scan of all options, then close study of a few, joining the rational and incremental models.

name: Multiple streams model
summary: Kingdon's model: policy changes when separate problem, policy and politics streams meet in an open policy window, helped by policy entrepreneurs.

name: Garbage can model
summary: Model of organisations as organised anarchies where problems, solutions, participants and choices mix, and decisions come when they meet by chance.
note: Co-written by Michael Cohen, James March and Johan Olsen.

name: Rule of law
summary: Dicey's three meanings: no punishment except for a breach of law proved in ordinary courts, equality of all before the law, and rights rooted in court decisions.

name: Delegated legislation
summary: Rules made by the executive under powers given by an Act of the legislature; Lord Hewart attacked its growth in The New Despotism (1929).

name: Ecological approach
summary: Studies administration through its environment; Gaus listed factors such as people, place, technology, ideas, catastrophe and personality.
note: Introduced by Gaus in Reflections on Public Administration (1947); developed by Riggs.

name: Development administration
summary: Administration of planned programmes for economic growth and social change in developing countries, as distinct from routine law-and-order administration.
note: Term credited to U.L. Goswami (1955); Weidner and Riggs developed the concept.

name: Anti-development thesis
summary: Critique by Escobar, Sachs, Esteva and others that 'development' is a Western discourse that harms local cultures, livelihoods and the environment.

name: Soft state
summary: Myrdal's term, from Asian Drama, for states that lack social discipline and fail to enforce their own laws and policies.

name: Good governance
summary: Governance that is participatory, consensus-oriented, accountable, transparent, responsive, effective, equitable and inclusive, and follows the rule of law.
note: Popularised by the World Bank from 1989; the eight features are the UN-ESCAP list.

name: Displacement of goals
summary: Merton's bureaucratic dysfunction, from 'Bureaucratic Structure and Personality', in which following rules becomes an end in itself and displaces the real goals.
note: Merton also used Thorstein Veblen's term 'trained incapacity'.

name: Contingency theory
summary: No one best way to organise: the right structure depends on environment, technology and size; developed by Burns and Stalker, Woodward, and Lawrence and Lorsch.

name: Achievement motivation theory
aliases: Need for achievement|Three needs theory|Acquired needs theory|McClelland's need theory
summary: McClelland's theory that people are driven by three learned needs: achievement, power and affiliation.

name: Expectancy theory
summary: Motivation depends on expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance brings reward) and valence (how much the reward is valued).

name: Fiedler's contingency model
aliases: Contingency model of leadership|LPC model|Least preferred co-worker
summary: Leader effectiveness depends on matching the leader's style, measured by the LPC scale, to how favourable the situation is.

name: Managerial Grid
aliases: The Managerial Grid|Leadership grid|Blake and Mouton grid
summary: Grid plotting concern for production against concern for people; team management (9,9) is the ideal style.
note: Developed with Jane Mouton.

name: Representative bureaucracy
summary: A civil service whose make-up mirrors the society it serves, which makes it more responsive to all groups.
note: Term from J. Donald Kingsley's Representative Bureaucracy (1944).

name: Steel frame
summary: Name for the Indian Civil Service, and later the all-India services, as the frame that holds the administration together.
note: Lloyd George used the phrase for the ICS in 1922; Patel defended the all-India services in 1949.

name: Planning-programming-budgeting system
summary: Budget system linking objectives, programmes and costs over several years; it began in the US Defense Department under McNamara.
note: Extended to all US federal agencies in 1965.

name: Zero-based budgeting
summary: Every activity must be justified afresh each year as a ranked decision package, as if the budget started from zero.
note: Developed by Peter Pyhrr at Texas Instruments; Jimmy Carter applied it in Georgia and then in the US federal government.

name: Performance budgeting
summary: Budget classified by functions, programmes and activities, linking the money spent to the work done and its results.
note: The term comes from the first Hoover Commission (1949).

name: Programme Evaluation and Review Technique
summary: Network technique for planning projects with optimistic, most likely and pessimistic time estimates; first used in the US Navy's Polaris missile programme.

name: Saptanga theory
summary: Kautilya's seven elements of the state: swami (king), amatya (ministers), janapada, durga (fort), kosha (treasury), danda (army) and mitra (ally).

name: Mansabdari system
summary: Akbar's system of ranks (zat and sawar) that fixed each noble's status, pay and the number of cavalry he kept.

name: Indicative planning
summary: Planning in which the state sets broad goals and guides the private sector through incentives, not fixed targets; India adopted it from the Eighth Plan (1992-97).

name: Hawthorne studies
summary: Studies at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago which found that social factors and group norms shaped output; the basis of the human relations school.
note: Mayo's Harvard team joined in 1927; many books date the studies 1927-32.

name: Minnowbrook Conference I
summary: Conference of young scholars at Syracuse University's Minnowbrook centre, sponsored by Dwight Waldo, that launched New Public Administration.

name: Minnowbrook Conference II
summary: Second Minnowbrook conference, held twenty years after the first to review public administration and the legacy of New Public Administration.

name: Minnowbrook Conference III
summary: Third Minnowbrook conference, forty years after the first, on the future of public administration and governance in a global setting.

name: Northcote-Trevelyan Report
summary: British report that called for civil service recruitment by open competitive examination and promotion on merit.
note: Dated November 1853; published in 1854.

name: Macaulay Committee Report
summary: Report on the Indian Civil Service recommending entry by open competitive examination; the first examination was held in London in 1855.

name: Fulton Committee Report
summary: British report on the civil service that criticised the cult of the generalist and led to a Civil Service Department and a Civil Service College.

name: Citizen's Charter
summary: UK programme under John Major that published service standards and means of redress; India adopted citizen's charters in 1997.

name: Ombudsman in Sweden
summary: Sweden set up the first parliamentary Ombudsman to hear citizens' complaints against officials, the model for later ombudsman bodies such as the Lokpal.

name: Ripon's Resolution on Local Self-Government
summary: Lord Ripon's resolution for elected local boards, which earned him the title 'father of local self-government in India'.

name: Office of the District Collector created
summary: Warren Hastings created the post of Collector to run revenue collection in each district, the base of district administration.

name: Planning Commission
summary: Set up by a Union Cabinet resolution, not by the Constitution or a statute, with the Prime Minister as its chairman.

name: NITI Aayog
summary: Replaced the Planning Commission as a policy think tank based on cooperative federalism.

name: Community Development Programme
summary: Launched in 55 project areas to develop rural areas through people's participation, with the block as the unit of work.

name: Balwantrai Mehta Committee
summary: Study team on the Community Development Programme that recommended three-tier Panchayati Raj; Rajasthan began it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.

name: Ashok Mehta Committee
summary: Committee on Panchayati Raj institutions that recommended a two-tier system of Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat.
note: Appointed in 1977; reported in 1978.

name: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act
summary: Gave panchayats constitutional status: Part IX, three tiers, reserved seats, five-year terms, State Election and Finance Commissions, and the Eleventh Schedule.
note: Passed in December 1992; in force from 24 April 1993.

name: 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
summary: Gave municipalities constitutional status: Part IXA, three types of municipality, the Twelfth Schedule, and district and metropolitan planning committees.
note: Passed in December 1992; in force from 1 June 1993.

name: First Administrative Reforms Commission
summary: Chaired first by Morarji Desai and then K. Hanumanthaiya; gave 20 reports, the first urging a Lokpal and Lokayuktas.

name: Second Administrative Reforms Commission
summary: Chaired first by Veerappa Moily and then V. Ramachandran; gave 15 reports, the first on the Right to Information.

name: Gorwala Report
summary: A.D. Gorwala's report to the Planning Commission on making administration efficient and clean enough to carry out the plans.

name: Central Vigilance Commission
summary: Set up by government resolution on the Santhanam Committee's advice to check corruption; made statutory by the CVC Act, 2003.

name: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act
summary: Set up a Lokpal at the Centre and required states to set up Lokayuktas to inquire into corruption by public servants.
note: Passed in December 2013; assent on 1 January 2014.

name: Right to Information Act
summary: Came fully into force, letting any citizen get information from public authorities, normally within 30 days.
note: Assented to on 15 June 2005; fully in force from 12 October 2005.

name: Kothari Committee
summary: Committee on recruitment policy whose three-stage examination (preliminary, main and interview) was used for the civil services from 1979.

name: National Police Commission
summary: Commission chaired by Dharma Vira that gave eight reports on police reform, including a draft Police Act.

name: Prakash Singh v. Union of India
summary: Supreme Court ordered police reforms, including State Security Commissions, fixed tenures and separating investigation from law and order.

name: National Human Rights Commission
summary: Set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 to inquire into violations of human rights.

name: Sarkaria Commission
summary: Commission on Centre-State relations chaired by Justice R.S. Sarkaria; it reviewed the Governor's role and Article 356 and favoured cooperative federalism.

name: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act
summary: Guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment a year to every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work.
note: In force from 2 February 2006; renamed after Mahatma Gandhi in 2009.

name: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956
summary: Reserved key industries in Schedule A for the state, making the public sector the leading force in industrial growth.

name: Central Administrative Tribunal
summary: Set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (based on Article 323A) to hear service disputes of central government employees.
